scope: Follow-up literature assessment of the four societal interpretations discussed in chat; no new analysis, reading or confirmation run.
assessment: None of the four broad societal interpretations has established priority for this project. Even the same tablet front occurring with different reverse stroke groups is explicitly described in Mukhopadhyay 2023. Potential additions are systematic measurements, controlled comparisons and source-checked chronological effects. Publication readiness and novelty of social interpretation are separate questions.

sources.title: Kenoyer, J. Mark and Richard H. Meadow (2010). Inscribed Objects from Harappa Excavations 1986–2007.
sources.locator: PDF pages 6–7, printed pages 6–7; chronological and seal-production discussions also inspected.
sources.observation: Explicitly contrasts mostly unique seals with copied and mould-duplicated tablets. Describes tablets in secondary deposits and the unresolved question of function. Reports chronological differences in seal forms. These precede our broad seal/tablet and temporal-change claims.
sources.status: Primary excavation synthesis; full-text passages inspected. Source already in the main review, with more specific passages added here.

sources.title: Mukhopadhyay, Bahata Ansumali (2023). Semantic scope of Indus inscriptions comprising taxation, trade and craft licensing, commodity control and access control: archaeological and script-internal evidence.
sources.locator: Section on reverse-side numerical expressions, especially paragraph referring to Figure 16b; abstract; discussion of Lothal sealings and Figure 22.
sources.observation: Explicitly describes identical obverse inscriptions paired with all three common reverse stroke constructs. Also discusses identical inscriptions across settlements and notes that identical sealing texts need not come from the same physical seal. The proposed licensing and tax semantics remain interpretations.
sources.status: Full-text passages inspected through the publisher's cookie-error fallback URL. Source already in the main review; the precise tablet precedent narrows our priority claim further.

sources.title: Rao, Rajesh P. N. (2018). The Indus Script and Economics. A Role for Indus Seals and Tablets in Rationing and Administration of Labor.
sources.observation: Develops the repetitive-transaction and ration-token hypothesis from miniature tablets and proposes functions for components of patterned texts. Explicitly calls for additional analysis and archaeological evidence. This precedes a general claim about organised recurring economic activities.
sources.status: Author-hosted copy of a scholarly volume chapter; full-text passages inspected.

sources.title: Yadav, Nisha (2013). Sensitivity of Indus Script to Site and Type of Object.
sources.locator: Scripta 5:67–103, especially section 4.1, printed pages 90–92, and section 5.
sources.observation: Measures differences among sites and object types in text lengths and sign usage, including Harappa versus Mohenjo-daro. Our fine-variant prediction test asks a different conditional question; its null result cannot establish general regional uniformity or refute these distributional results.
sources.status: Primary journal article; abstract and relevant full-text sections inspected. Newly added to this review.

sources.title: Jamison, Gregg, Akinori Uesugi and Yuji Yamaguchi (2023). Unicorns and seals: New multivariate approaches to exploring patterned stylistic variation in the Indus Civilization.
sources.locator: Publisher abstract and public methods, discussion and conclusion snippets.
sources.observation: Reports attribute and correspondence analysis of 827 unicorn seals from 24 sites, with fine stylistic and diachronic variation. Requires comparison before any broad shared-conventions or regional-variation claim.
sources.status: Primary publisher record and excerpts inspected; full article was not inspected in this follow-up.

publication_assessment.potential_addition: The defined population of 417 objects, 17 matched companion-face classes with variable tall-stroke groups, and decomposition of copying and face-role effects.
publication_assessment.limitation: The structural pattern and proposed functions have close predecessors. Preserving face roles removes the corrected sign-pair result, so the original result cannot support special semantic binding.
publication_assessment.needed: Audit physical objects and all faces, distinguish copies from independent production, quantify uncertainty, and test a frozen model on previously unexamined objects. Specific social function requires independently coded use histories, attachment evidence, residues, wear or cancellation, and secure archaeological contexts.
publication_assessment.verdict: Possible structural or methods contribution after source audit; a new institutional interpretation needs physical evidence.

publication_assessment.potential_addition: Reproducible length-dependent repetition measurements and matched comparisons with readable seal corpora.
publication_assessment.limitation: The broad contrast is explicit in Kenoyer and Meadow 2010. Uniqueness of long texts alone does not distinguish personal names from offices, commodities or transaction descriptions.
publication_assessment.needed: Match readable comparators and null models for length, sign inventory, frequency and sample size; resolve object aliases and duplicates; test discriminating predictions on new contextualised material.
publication_assessment.verdict: Supporting result at present; potential comparative paper.

publication_assessment.potential_addition: Audited distributions of repeated texts and specialist-confirmed identification of independently carved matrices carrying the same text.
publication_assessment.limitation: Distant identical inscriptions are prior evidence. The primary locality test is not significant; failure of the narrow regional variant prediction does not demonstrate uniformity.
publication_assessment.needed: Specialist image or object adjudication, matched date and manufacture, excavation context and vessel or sealing attachment evidence. Separate movement of goods, movement of a seal and copying of a formula. Replicate regional tests on unused objects and compare directly with Yadav 2013 and stylistic studies.
publication_assessment.verdict: Possible specialist note after physical confirmation; institutions or networks require broader context.

publication_assessment.claim: Harappa changed its inscription practices while retaining common endings
publication_assessment.potential_addition: Within-trench measurements of length and sign-inventory changes in Mound F, including growth among square seals.
publication_assessment.limitation: Chronological change is prior work. Period mappings and context integrity require audit; graphic-variant change depends on Trench I. The closing-stock interval allows a substantial decline and cannot establish invariant grammar. Public overlapping approaches are recorded in the main review.
publication_assessment.needed: Archaeological audit of original strata and period assignments, treatment of residual and redeposited objects, format and dimension controls, influence reporting and prospective replication on independently dated HARP material. A claim of expanding administration needs changes in independently identified activities or institutional contexts.
publication_assessment.verdict: Strongest candidate for a focused archaeological article after chronological validation.

data_update.coverage_change: None. Bibliographic evidence only; no third-party raw files acquired or redistributed.

retrospective: Targeted searches recovered a direct tablet-face precedent and a regional-distribution study omitted from the earlier short synthesis. Publisher access required a cookie-error fallback. The follow-up narrows priority claims and separates publication of a measured pattern from identification of its historical function. Frozen experiment outputs were not changed.
limits: Targeted review, not an exhaustive priority search. Book-length studies were not comprehensively checked, calculations in prior publications were not replicated, and no new epigraphic or archaeological verification was performed.
